questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The standard electrode potential ($E^\circ$) for the half-cell reaction $\text{Fe}^{3+}+e^-\rightarrow\text{Fe}^{2+}$ at $298$ K is
(Given: $E^\circ(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe})=-0.04$ V and $E^\circ(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe})=-0.44$ V at $298$ K)
questions.solution:
The given half-cell reactions are:

$\text{Fe}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}$, $E^\circ_1 = -0.04$ V
$\Delta G^\circ_1 = -n_1FE^\circ_1 = -3 \times F \times (-0.04) = 0.12F$

$\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}$, $E^\circ_2 = -0.44$ V
$\Delta G^\circ_2 = -n_2FE^\circ_2 = -2 \times F \times (-0.44) = 0.88F$

The required half-cell reaction is:
$\text{Fe}^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$

This reaction can be obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first reaction:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2$

$-1 \times F \times E^\circ_3 = 0.12F - 0.88F$

$-FE^\circ_3 = -0.76F$

$E^\circ_3 = +0.76$ V

Answer: $+0.76$ V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For a salt $\text{XY}$, which is a strong electrolyte, the plot of $\Lambda_m$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ has a slope of $-90.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-3/2}$ L$^{1/2}$ at $298$ K. At $0.01$ M concentration of $\text{XY}$, the value of $\Lambda_m$ is $145.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$. The limiting molar conductivity of $\text{Y}^-$ ion ($\lambda^0_{Y^-}$, in S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$) at $298$ K will be
(Given : $\lambda^0_{X^+}=74.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to the Debye-Huckel-Onsager equation for strong electrolytes:

$\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^0 - A\sqrt{c}$

The slope of the plot of $\Lambda_m$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ is $-A$.

Given slope $= -90.0$, we have $A = 90.0$.

At $c = 0.01$ M, $\sqrt{c} = 0.1$ M$^{1/2}$.

Substituting the given values into the equation:

$145.0 = \Lambda_m^0 - 90.0 \times 0.1$

$145.0 = \Lambda_m^0 - 9.0$

$\Lambda_m^0 = 154.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$

According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions:

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{XY}) = \lambda^0_{\text{X}^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{Y}^-}$

$154.0 = 74.0 + \lambda^0_{\text{Y}^-}$

$\lambda^0_{\text{Y}^-} = 154.0 - 74.0 = 80.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$

Answer: $80.0$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: From the following select the one which is not an example of corrosion.
options: Production of hydrogen by electrolysis of water
Development of green coating on copper and bronze ornaments
questions.solution:
Corrosion slowly coats the surfaces of metallic objects with oxides or other salts of the metal. The rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver, development of green coating on copper and bronze are some of the examples of corrosion.
- Production of $\mathrm{H}_2$ by electrolysis of water is an example of electrolytic cell.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A solution of copper sulphate is electrolysed for $10$ minutes with a current of $1.5$ amperes. The mass of copper deposited at cathode is :
(Given : Molar mass of $\text{Cu} = 63$ g mol$^{-1}$; $1$ F $= 96487$ C mol$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The reaction at the cathode is $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$.

The quantity of charge $Q$ passed through the solution is given by $Q = I \times t$.

Substituting the given values:
$Q = 1.5 \text{ A} \times (10 \times 60) \text{ s} = 900 \text{ C}$

From Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass of copper deposited is:
$m = \dfrac{M \times Q}{n \times F}$

Here, $M = 63 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$, $n = 2$, and $F = 96487 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$.

$m = \dfrac{63 \times 900}{2 \times 96487}$

$m = \dfrac{56700}{192974} \approx 0.2938 \text{ g}$

Answer: $0.2938$ g

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Molar conductance of an electrolyte increases with dilution according to the equation:
$\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}-\mathrm{A} \sqrt{\mathrm{c}}$
Which of the following statements are true?
(A) This equation applies to both strong and weak electrolytes.
(B) Value of the constant A depends upon the nature of the solvent.
(C) Value of constant $\mathrm{A}$ is same for both $\mathrm{BaCl}_2$ and $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$.
(D) Value of constant $A$ is same for both $\mathrm{BaCl}_2$ and $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_2$.
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
questions.solution:
$\Lambda_m=\Lambda_m^{\circ}-A \sqrt{c}$
- For strong electrolytes, $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ increases slowly with dilution.
- The value of ' $A$ ' depends on the type of electrolyte.
- All electrolytes of particular type have the same value for 'A'
e.g. $\mathrm{BaCl}_2$ and $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_2 \rightarrow 2-1$ electrolytes

The $E^{\ominus}$ values for
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{Al}^{+} / \mathrm{Al}=+0.55 \mathrm{ V} \text{ and } \mathrm{Tl}^{+} / \mathrm{TI}=-0.34 \mathrm{ V} \\ & \mathrm{Al}^{3+} / \mathrm{Al}=-1.66 \mathrm{ V} \text{ and } \mathrm{Tl}^{3+} / \mathrm{TI}=+1.26 \mathrm{ V}\end{aligned}$
Identify the incorrect statement.
options: $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$ is a good reducing agent than $\mathrm{Tl}^{1+}$.
questions.solution:
(1) $\mathrm{Al}^{+}$is unstable in solution because $\mathrm{SRP} of \mathrm{Al}^{+} / \mathrm{Al}$ is positive hence, it will get reduced in solution.
(2)
$\begin{array}{ll}\mathrm{Tl} / \mathrm{Tl}^{+}=$+0.34 & ($\mathrm{SOP}) \\ \mathrm{Tl} / \mathrm{Tl}^{3+}=$-1.26 & ($\mathrm{SOP})\end{array}$
Since, SOP TI/TI $>$ TI/T1 ${ }^{+}$
Hence, $\mathrm{TI}$ will get oxidised to $\mathrm{Tl}^{+}easily than \mathrm{Tl}^{3+}

Since $\begin{aligned} $\mathrm{Tl}^{3+}+$2 $\mathrm{e}^{-}$ \rightarrow $\mathrm{Tl}^{+}$ ; $\mathrm{E}=\frac{3 \times 1.26+0.34}{2}$ \\ =+2.04\end{aligned}$
Hence, \mathrm{Tl}^{3+}$is better oxidising agent not reducing agent

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The conductivity of centimolar solution of $KCl$ at $25 ° C$ is $0 . 0210{ohm}^{- 1}{cm}^{- 1}$ and the resistance of the cell containing the solution at $25 ° C$ is $60ohm$. The value of cell constant is
questions.solution:
Conductivity$\left(κ\right) = 0 . 0210{ohm}^{- 1}{cm}^{- 1}$

Resistance$\left(R\right) = 60ohm$

The relation between specific conductance or conductivity and resistance is

$κ = \dfrac{1}{R}\dfrac{l}{a}$

In the above equation $\dfrac{l}{a}$ is the cell constant.

$\dfrac{l}{a} = κ \times R$

$⇒ \dfrac{l}{a} = 0 . 0210 \times 60 = 1 . 26{cm}^{- 1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two half cell reactions are given below :
$\mathrm{CO}^{3+}+\mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Co}^{2+}, \mathrm{E}^{\circ} \mathrm{Co}^{2+} / \mathrm{Co}^{3+}=-1.81 \mathrm{~V}$
$2 \mathrm{Al}^{3+}+6 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{s}), \mathrm{E}^{\mathrm{o}} \mathrm{Al} / \mathrm{Al}^{3+}=+1.66 \mathrm{~V}$
The standard EMF of a cell with feasible redox reaction will be :
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is written as :
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{E}^{\circ} \mathrm{Co}^{2+} / \mathrm{Co}^{3+}=-1.81 \mathrm{~V}(\mathrm{SOP}) \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{E}^{\circ} \mathrm{Co}^{3+} / \mathrm{Co}^{2+}=+1.81 \mathrm{~V} \text{ (SRP) } \\
& \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{A} / / \mathrm{Al}^{3+}}^{\circ}=+1.66 \mathrm{~V}(\mathrm{SOP}) \\
& \therefore \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Al}^{3+} / \mathrm{Al}}^{\circ}=-1.66 \mathrm{~V}(\mathrm{SRP}) \\
&
\end{aligned}$
Here $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}$ is given in standard Reduction Potential
$\therefore \mathrm{Co}^{3+} / \mathrm{Co}$ will undergo reduction acting as cathode and $\mathrm{Al}^{3+} / \mathrm{Al}$ will undergo oxidation acting as anode.
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \mathrm{E}_{\text{cell }}^{\circ} & =\mathrm{E}_{\text{cathode (Red.) }}^{\circ}-\mathrm{E}_{\text{Anode (oxide) }}^{\circ} \\
\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell }}^{\circ} & =1.81-(-1.66) \\
\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell }}^{\circ} & =+3.47 \mathrm{~V}
\end{aligned}$

${MnO}_{4}^{-} + 8{H}^{+} + 5{e}^{-} \to {Mn}^{2 +} + 4{H}_{2}O$,

${E}_{{Mn}^{2 +} / {MnO}_{4}^{-}}^{o} = - 1 . 510V$

$\dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2} + 2{H}^{+} + 2{e}^{-} \to {H}_{2}O$

${E}_{{O}_{2} / {H}_{2}O}^{o} = + 1 . 223V$

Will the permanganate ion, ${MnO}_{4}^{-}$ liberate ${O}_{2}$ from water in the presence of an acid?

The reaction between ${MnO}_{4}^{-}$ and ${H}_{2}O$ is

${E}^{o}$ for the cell reaction:-

$E ° = {E}_{{MnO}_{4}^{-} / {Mn}^{+ 2}}^{o} + {E}_{{H}_{2}O / {O}_{2}}^{o}$

$= 1 . 510V - 1 . 223V$

${E}^{o} = + 0 . 287V$

As $E °$ of the cell reaction is positive, so this reaction is feasible. Therefore permanganate ion ${MnO}_{4}^{-}$ liberate ${O}_{2}$ from water in presence of an acid.

Hence, option D is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
At $298K$, the standard electrode potentials of ${Cu}^{2 +} / Cu, {Zn}^{2 +} / Zn, {Fe}^{2 +} / Fe$ and ${Ag}^{+} / Ag$ are $0 . 34V$, $- 0 . 76V$, $- 0 . 44V$ and $0 . 80V$, respectively.

On the basis of standard electrode potential, predict which of the following reaction cannot occur?
options: ${CuSO}_{4} ( aq ) + Fe ( s ) \to {FeSO}_{4} ( aq ) + Cu ( s )$
${FeSO}_{4} ( aq ) + Zn ( s ) \to {ZnSO}_{4} ( aq ) + Fe ( s )$
${CuSO}_{4} ( aq ) + Zn ( s ) \to {ZnSO}_{4} ( aq ) + Cu ( s )$
questions.solution:
The given standard reduction potentials of $Zn, Cu, Ag and Fe$ are;

$E° \dfrac{{Zn}^{2 +}}{Zn} = - 0 . 76V, E° \dfrac{{Cu}^{2 +}}{cu} = 0 . 34VE° \dfrac{{Ag}^{+}}{Ag} = 0 . 80V, andE° \dfrac{{Fe}^{2 +}}{Fe} = - 0 . 44V$

The condition for reaction to occur, $E{°}_{Cell} = {\left(E{°}_{SRP}\right)}_{reductionreaction} - {\left(E{°}_{SRP}\right)}_{oxidationreaction}$ must have the positive value.

$\left(A\right){Cu}^{2 +}\left(aq\right) + Fe \to Cu + {Fe}^{2 +}\left(aq\right)$

$E{°}_{Cell} = 0 . 34 + 0 . 44E{°}_{Cell} = 0 . 78V$

$\left(B\right)Zn + {Fe}^{2 +}\left(aq\right) \to {Zn}^{2 +}\left(aq\right) + Fe$

$E{°}_{Cell} = - 0 . 44 + 0 . 76E{°}_{Cell} = + 0 . 32V$

$\left(C\right){Cu}^{2 +}\left(aq\right) + 2Ag \to 2{Ag}^{+}\left(aq\right) + Cu$

$E{°}_{Cell} = 0 . 34 - 0 . 80E{°}_{Cell} = - 0 . 46V$

questions.q:
Find the emf of the cell in which the following reaction takes place at $298K$

$Ni ( s ) + 2{Ag}^{+} ( 0 . 001M ) \to {Ni}^{2 +} ( 0 . 001M ) + 2Ag ( s )$

(Given that $E{°}_{cell} = 1 . 05V, \dfrac{2 . 303RT}{F} = 0 . 059$ at $298K$)
questions.solution:
Given reaction: $Ni ( s ) + 2{Ag}^{+} ( 0 . 001M ) \to {Ni}^{2 +} ( 0 . 001M ) + 2Ag ( s )$

Applying Nernst equation we have:
${E}_{\left(cell\right)} = {E}_{\left(cell\right)}^{0} - \dfrac{2 . 303RT}{nF}log\dfrac{\left[{Ni}^{2 +}\right] [ Ag ]}{{\left[{Ag}^{+}\right]}^{2} [ Ni ]}$
Active mass of solid is taken to be unity so $\left[Ni\left(s\right)\right] = \left[Ag\left(s\right)\right] = 1$
${E}_{\left(cell\right)} = {E}_{\left(cell\right)}^{0} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}log\dfrac{\left[N{i}^{2 +}\right]}{{\left[A{g}^{+}\right]}^{2}}$
$= 1.05 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2}log\dfrac{\left(0.001\right)}{{\left(0.001\right)}^{2}}$
$= 1.05 - 0.0295log (1\times {10}^{3} )$
$= 1.05 - 0.0295 \times 3$
$= 0.9615V$

Therefore, the emf of the cell is $0 . 9615V$.

Note: Question is modified little bit for academic accuracy. $E{°}_{cell} = 1 . 05VinplaceofE{°}_{cell} = 10 . 5V$ as given in NEET 2022 paper.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate emf of the half cell given below :
$\text{Pt (s)} | \text{H}_2 \text{(g, 2 atm)} | \text{HCl (aq, 0.02 M)}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{H}_2/\text{H}^{+}} = 0$ V
$\left(\text{Given}: \dfrac{2.303\ RT}{F} = 0.059, \log 2 = 0.3010\right)$
questions.solution:
The given half-cell is represented as an oxidation electrode: $\text{Pt (s)} | \text{H}_2 \text{(g)} | \text{H}^{+} \text{(aq)}$.

The corresponding oxidation half-cell reaction is:
$\text{H}_2 \text{(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{H}^{+} \text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-}$

Using the Nernst equation for the oxidation potential:
$E = E^{\circ}_{\text{H}_2/\text{H}^{+}} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}{P_{\text{H}_2}}$

Given values:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{H}_2/\text{H}^{+}} = 0$ V
$n = 2$
$[\text{H}^{+}] = 0.02$ M (since HCl is a strong monoprotic acid)
$P_{\text{H}_2} = 2$ atm

Substituting the values into the Nernst equation:
$E = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{(0.02)^2}{2}$

$E = -0.0295 \log \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-4}}{2}$

$E = -0.0295 \log (2 \times 10^{-4})$

$E = -0.0295 (\log 2 + \log 10^{-4})$

$E = -0.0295 (0.3010 - 4)$

$E = -0.0295 \times (-3.699)$

$E = 0.10912$ V $\approx 0.109$ V

Answer: $0.109$ V

questions.solution:
More negative the value of standard reduction potential, higher is the reduction power.

Thus, the correct decreasing order of reducing power of the metal is
$$

& \mathrm{Cr}>\mathrm{Ag} \\
& \left(\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} / \mathrm{Cr}}^0=-0.74 \mathrm{~V}\right) \quad\left(\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}}^0 / \mathrm{Ag}=0.80 \mathrm{~V}\right) \\
&
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Among the following, the plot that correctly represents the conductometric titration of $0 . 05M$ ${H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ with $0 . 1M{NH}_{4}OH$ is
questions.solution:
The principle of conductometric titration is based on the fact that during the titration one of the ions is replaced by other and invariably these two ions differ in the ionic conductivity.

In the conductometric titration of $0 . 05M$ ${H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ with $0 . 1M{NH}_{4}OH$, initially the fast moving ${H}^{+}$ ion get neutralised as ${H}_{2}O$ and is replaced by slow moving ${NH}_{4}^{+}$ ion up to neutralisation point. After neutralisation point, weak electrolyte ${NH}_{4}OH$ is added gradually, which do not affect the conductance.

options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

$\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}+2 e^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}$
$\therefore$ Quantity of electricity required $=2 \mathrm{~F}$
Thus, two mole of electrons produce one mole of $\mathrm{Mg}$. It can be concluded that if $n, c=1 \mathrm{~mol}$ electrons are involved in the electrod reaction, the passage of $n$ Faradays of electricity will liberate one mole of the substance, i.e. the charge on one mole of electrons is one Faraday.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For $KI$, molar conductivity increases steeply with dilution.

Statement II: For carbonic acid, molar conductivity increases slowly with dilution. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
For strong electrolytes, ${∧}_{m}$ increases slowly with dilution and can be represented by the equation:

${∧}_{m} = {∧}_{m}^{o} - Ac\dfrac{1}{2}$

It can be seen that if we plot ${∧}_{m}$ against $c\dfrac{1}{2}$, We obtain a straight line with intercept equal to ${∧}_{m}$ and slope equal to '$- A$'. The value of the constant '$A$' for a given solvent and temperature depends on the type of electrolyte. $KI$ is a strong electrolyte.

Weak electrolytes like carbonic acid and have lower degree of dissociation at higher concentrations and hence for such electrolytes, the change in ${∧}_{m}$ with dilution is due to increase in the degree of dissociation and consequently the number of ions in total volume of solution that contains $1mol$ of electrolyte. In such cases ${∧}_{m}$ increases steeply on dilution, especially near lower concentrations. Therefore, ${∧}_{m}^{o}$ cannot be obtained by extrapolation of ${∧}_{m}$ to zero concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement-I : In electrochemical cells, Gibbs energy of spontaneous redox reaction is converted into electrical work.
Statement-II : Gibb's energy can be calculated by using \(\Delta \mathrm{G}=-\mathrm{nFE}\) & it is an intensive property. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both statement I and II are incorrect.
Both statement I and II are correct.
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct.
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
questions.solution:
Statement-I:
In electrochemical cells, spontaneous redox reactions generate an electric potential difference. The Gibbs energy (\($\Delta \mathrm{G}$\)) of the reaction is converted into electrical work, which is measured as the electromotive force (EMF) of the cell. This is a fundamental principle of electrochemistry.
Statement-II:
The Gibbs energy (\($\Delta \mathrm{G}$\)) can indeed be calculated using the equation:
\($\Delta \mathrm{G}=-\mathrm{nFE}$\)
where:
n = number of electrons transferred
F = Faraday constant (\(96485 $\mathrm{C}$/ $\mathrm{mol}$\))
E = cell potential (in volts)
Gibbs energy is an extensive property, but \($\Delta \mathrm{G}$\) (change in Gibbs energy) is an intensive property, as it is independent of the system size.
Since both statements are correct, the answer is option (2).
Intensive properties are independent of the system size or amount of substance, unlike extensive properties which depend on the amount of substance. Examples of intensive properties include temperature, pressure, and concentration.

questions.q:
Any redox reaction would occur spontaneously, if :
(a) the free energy change \((\Delta G)\) is negative.
(b) the \(\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}\) is positive.
(c) the cell EMF is negative.
(d) the cell EMF is positive.
questions.solution:
For a spontaneous redox reaction:
(a) The free energy change (\($\Delta \mathrm{G}$\)) must be negative. This indicates that the reaction is thermodynamically favorable.
\($\Delta \mathrm{G} \lt$0\) (spontaneous)
(d) The cell EMF (Electromotive Force) must be positive. A positive EMF indicates that the reaction can generate an electric potential difference.
Ecell > 0 (spontaneous)
The other options are incorrect:
(b) \($\Delta \mathrmG^{{}^{\circ}}$\) (standard free energy change) being positive indicates a non-spontaneous reaction.
(c) A negative cell EMF indicates that the reaction is non-spontaneous.
Note: \($\Delta \mathrmG^{{}^{\circ}}=-$n $\mathrm{FE}^{{}^{\circ}}$\), where \(\mathrmE^{{}^{\circ}}\) is the standard cell potential. A positive \(\mathrmE^{{}^{\circ}}\) corresponds to a negative \($\Delta$G^{{}^{\circ}}\).

questions.q:
An aqueous solution of X is added slowly to an aqueous solution of Y as shown in List I. The variation in conductivity of these reactions is given in List II. Match List I with List II and select the correct using answer the code given below the lists :
 
  List I   List II
a.  $\begin{array}{ll}{\left({\text{C}}_{2} {\text{H}}_{5}\right)}_{3} \text{N} + {\text{CH}}_{3} \text{COOH} \\ \text{X} \text{Y}\end{array}$ p.  Conductivity decreases and then 
increases 
b.  $\begin{array}{ll}\text{KI} \left(0 \text{.} 1 \text{M}\right) + {\text{AgNO}}_{3} \left(0 \text{.} 0 1 \text{M}\right) \\ \text{X} \text{Y}\end{array}$ q.  Conductivity decreases and then
does not change much 
c.  $\begin{array}{ll}{\text{CH}}_{3} \text{COOH} + \text{KOH} \\ \text{X} \text{Y}\end{array}$ r.  Conductivity increases and then
does not change much
d.  $\begin{array}{ll}\text{NaOH} + \text{HI} \\ \text{X} \text{Y}\end{array}$ s.  Conductivity does not change much and 
then increases
questions.solution:
p)  (C2H5)3 N added to CH3COOH
(C2H5)3 NH+ and CH3COO- ions generated in solution, conductivity increases & then remains constant as (C2H5)3 N is not dissociated when in excess.

q)  KIeq added to AgNO3
$\left[{\text{Ag}}_{\text{(aq)}}^{+} + {\text{NO}_{3 \text{(aq)}}^{-}\right] + \text{KI} ⟶ \left[{\text{K}}_{\text{(aq)}}^{+} + {\text{NO}_{3 \text{(aq)}}^{-}\right] + \text{AgI}$
$\left({\text{Ag}}^{+} \text{$ and $} {\text{NO}_{3}^{-}\right)$  ions replaced by $\left({\text{K}}_{\text{(aq)}}^{+} \text{$ and $} {\text{NO}_{3 \text{(aq)}}^{-}\right)$
conductivity does not change till complete precipitation but later on with additional KI(aq) added conductivity will increase.

r)  On addition of acetic acid to KOH. KOH fully dissociated replaced by
${\text{CH}_{3} \text{COOH} + \left({\text{K}}^{+} + {\text{OH}}^{-}\right) ⟶ \left[{\text{CH}_{3} {\text{COO}}^{-} + {\text{K}}^{+}\right] + {\text{H}_{2} \text{O}$
The net result is replacement of OH- by CH3COO- ions whose ionic mobility is less so conductivity will decrease first and then will not change much due to addition of CH3COOH(in excess) which will not be dissociated
 
s)  On addition of NaOH to HI $\left({\text{H}}_{\text{(aq)}}^{+} + {\text{I}}_{\text{(aq)}}^{-}\right) + \text{NaOH} ⟶ \left({\text{Na}}^{+} + {\text{I}}^{-}\right) + {\text{H}_{2} \text{O}$
there will be replacement of H+ by Na+ whose mobility is less than H+ which means conductivity will decrease first & then due to adding NaOH which is a strong electrolyte which fully dissociates, so conductivity will increase.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II \(
amp; List - I (Cell)amp;amp; List - II (Use/Property/Reaction)
A.amp; Leclanche cellamp; I.amp; Converts energy of combustion into electrical
energy
B.amp; Ni-Cd cellamp; II.amp; Does not involve any ion in solution and is used
in hearing aids
C.amp; Fuel cellamp; III.amp; Rechargeable
D.amp; Mercury cellamp; IV.amp; Reaction at anode Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+}+2 \mathrme^{-}
\) Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
- A. Leclanche cell (Dry cell): This is the most common type of primary cell. At the zinc anode, the reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}+2 e^{-}\). Therefore, A matches with IV.
- B. Ni-Cd cell: This is a secondary cell, meaning it is rechargeable. Therefore, B matches with III.
- C. Fuel cell: These cells are designed to convert the energy from the combustion of fuels (like hydrogen) directly into electrical energy. Therefore, C matches with I.
- D. Mercury cell: This is a small, compact primary cell that is commonly used in devices like hearing aids. It is designed to have a constant voltage and a long lifespan, and its internal chemistry doesn't involve ions in solution, making it suitable for compact sealed devices. Therefore, D matches with II.
The correct option is (4) A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

\(
List-IList-II

ZnO(s)+Hg(l)		IIDischarging of secondary battery

Pb(s)+PbO_2 (s)+2 H_2 SO_4(aq)		IIIFuel cell
D2 H_2 (g)+O_2 (g) \rightarrow
2 H_2 O(l)		IVCharging of secondary battery
\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: $A - I, B - II, C - III, C - IV$
$A - IV, B - I, C - IV, C - III$
$A - II, B - I, C - IV, C - III$
$A - II, B - I, C - III, C - IV$
questions.solution:
(a)$Cd\left(s\right) + 2Ni{\left(OH\right)}_{3}\left(s\right) \to CdO\left(s\right) + 2Ni{\left(OH\right)}_{2}\left(s\right) + {H}_{2}O\left(l\right)$ 
Discharge of secondary Battery

(b)$Zn\left(Hg\right) + HgO\left(s\right) \to ZnO\left(s\right) + Hg\left(l\right)$ 
(Primary Battery Mercury cell)

(c) $2{PbSO}_{4}\left(s\right) + 2{H}_{2}O\left(l\right) \to Pb\left(s\right) + {PbO}_{2}\left(s\right) + 2{H}_{2}{SO}_{4}\left(aq\right)$ Charging of secondary Battery

(d) $2{H}_{2}\left(g\right) + {O}_{2}\left(g\right) \to 2{H}_{2}O\left(l\right) -$ Fuel cell

Mercury cell, suitable for low current devices like hearing aids, watches, etc. consists of zinc - mercury amalgam as anode and a paste of $HgO$ and carbon as the cathode. The electrolyte is a paste of $KOH$ and $ZnO$. The electrode reactions for the cell are given below:

Anode: $Zn\left(Hg\right) + 2{OH}^{-} \to ZnO\left(s\right) + {H}_{2}O + 2{e}^{-}$

Cathode: $HgO + {H}_{2}O + 2{e}^{-} \to Hg\left(l\right) + 2{OH}^{-}$

Another important secondary cell is the nickel-cadmium cell which has longer life than the lead storage cell but more expensive to manufacture.

The overall reaction during discharge is:

$Cd\left(s\right) + 2Ni{\left(OH\right)}_{3}\left(s\right) \to CdO\left(s\right) + 2Ni{\left(OH\right)}_{2}\left(s\right) + {H}_{2}O\left(l\right)$

Fuel cell using ${H}_{2}$ and ${O}_{2}$ produces electricity.

Cathode: ${O}_{2}\left(g\right) + 2{H}_{2}O\left(l\right) + 4{e}^{-} \to 4{OH}^{-}\left(aq\right)$

Anode: $2{H}_{2}\left(g\right) + 4{OH}^{-}\left(aq\right) \to 4{H}_{2}O\left(l\right) + 4{e}^{-}$

Overall reaction being:

$2{H}_{2}\left(g\right) + {O}_{2}\left(g\right) \to 2{H}_{2}O\left(l\right)$

(ii) Cell reaction of lead storage battery during recharge -

The reverse of oxidation at anode during discharge is the reduction reaction at cathode during recharging.

${Pb}_{\left(aq\right)}^{2 +} + 2{e}^{-} \to {Pb}_{\left(s\right)}$

${PbSO}_{4\left(s\right)} \to {Pb}_{\left(aq\right)}^{2 +} + {SO}_{4\left(aq\right)}^{2 -}$

Final Reaction: ${PbSO}_{4\left(s\right)} + 2{e}^{-} \to {Pb}_{\left(s\right)} + {SO}_{4\left(aq\right)}^{2 -}$

(iv)Solubility of sparingly soluble salt(S)Decreases with dilution
\)
questions.solution:
(i) Molar conductivity is defined as the conductivity of a solution containing one mole of an electrolyte. Therefore, it is directly related to:
P) Molarity
(ii) Conductivity of an electrolyte solution increases with concentration, but molar conductivity increases with dilution and reaches a limiting value. This limiting value is:
R) Limiting molar conductivity
(iii) Degree of dissociation (\($\alpha$\)) is related to the molar conductivity (\(\lambda $\mathrm{m}$\)) and limiting molar conductivity (\(\lambda^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{m}$\)) through the equation:
\($\alpha=\lambda \mathrm{m}$/ \lambda^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{m}$\)
Hence, it is related to:
Q) Conductivity / Molar Conductivity
(iv) Solubility of sparingly soluble salts:
Decreases with dilution is not accurate in this context; instead, solubility product (Ksp) remains constant. However, considering the closest match:
S) Decreases with [common ion] concentration or Increases with dilution isn't listed, but S matches best.
So, the correct matches are:
(i) \($\rightarrow \mathrm{P}$\)
(ii) \( → R\)
(iii) \( → Q\)
(iv) \( → S\)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The plots of molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) versus the square root of concentration ($\sqrt{c}$) for the strong electrolytes $\text{HCl}$, $\text{NaA}$, and $\text{NaCl}$ yield straight lines with y-intercepts of $426.0$, $91.0$, and $126.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$, respectively, at $298$ K. If the molar conductivity of a $0.001$ M solution of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ at the same temperature is $39.1$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$, what is its degree of dissociation?
questions.solution:
For strong electrolytes, the y-intercept of the $\Lambda_m$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ plot corresponds to the limiting molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m^0$).

Thus, we have:
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{HCl}) = 426.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NaA}) = 91.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NaCl}) = 126.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$

According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions, the limiting molar conductivity of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ can be calculated as:

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{HA}) = \Lambda_m^0(\text{HCl}) + \Lambda_m^0(\text{NaA}) - \Lambda_m^0(\text{NaCl})$

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{HA}) = 426.0 + 91.0 - 126.0 = 391.0$ S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$

The degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) is given by the ratio of molar conductivity at a given concentration to the limiting molar conductivity:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^0}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{39.1}{391.0} = 0.10$

Answer: $0.10$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The molar conductivity of a $0.018 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$ solution of acetic acid is $39.05 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$. If the limiting molar conductivities of $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ ions are $349.6 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $40.9 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively, the acid dissociation constant ($K_a$) of acetic acid is:
questions.solution:
Limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid is:

$\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-)$
$\Lambda_m^\circ = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Degree of dissociation, $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{39.05}{390.5} = 0.1$

Using Ostwald's dilution law, the acid dissociation constant $K_a$ is:
$K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$
$K_a = \dfrac{0.018 \times (0.1)^2}{1 - 0.1}$
$K_a = \dfrac{0.018 \times 0.01}{0.9} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-4}}{0.9} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$

Answer: $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$
questions.question: The molar conductivity of a $0.018 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$ solution of acetic acid is $39.05 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$. If the limiting molar conductivities of $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ ions are $349.6 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $40.9 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively, the acid dissociation constant ($K_a$) of acetic acid is:
questions.explanation:
Limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid is:

$\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-)$
$\Lambda_m^\circ = 349.6 + 40.9 = 390.5 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Degree of dissociation, $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{39.05}{390.5} = 0.1$

Using Ostwald's dilution law, the acid dissociation constant $K_a$ is:
$K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$
$K_a = \dfrac{0.018 \times (0.1)^2}{1 - 0.1}$
$K_a = \dfrac{0.018 \times 0.01}{0.9} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-4}}{0.9} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$

Answer: $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Three electrolytic cells A, B, and C containing solutions of $\text{ZnSO}_4$, $\text{AgNO}_3$, and $\text{CuSO}_4$, respectively, are connected in series. A steady current is passed through them until a certain amount of metal is deposited at the respective cathodes. The ratio of the number of moles of Zn, Ag, and Cu deposited is :
questions.solution:
When cells are connected in series, the same quantity of electricity ($Q$) passes through each cell.

According to Faraday's laws of electrolysis, the number of moles of a substance deposited is given by:
$\text{Moles} = \dfrac{Q}{n \times F}$

Since $Q$ and $F$ are constant for all three cells, the number of moles deposited is inversely proportional to the valency ($n$-factor) of the metal ion.

The reduction reactions at the cathodes are:
$\text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Zn} \quad (n = 2)$
$\text{Ag}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag} \quad (n = 1)$
$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu} \quad (n = 2)$

The ratio of the number of moles of Zn, Ag, and Cu deposited is:
$\dfrac{1}{2} : \dfrac{1}{1} : \dfrac{1}{2}$

Multiplying by 2 to get whole numbers, the ratio is $1 : 2 : 1$.

Answer: $1 : 2 : 1$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The limiting molar conductivities of $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, $\text{BaCl}_2$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ are given as $x$, $y$ and $z \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The limiting molar conductivity of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ in $\text{S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ will be:
questions.solution:
According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions:

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{Ba(OH)}_2) = \lambda^0_{\text{Ba}^{2+}} + 2\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} = x$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{BaCl}_2) = \lambda^0_{\text{Ba}^{2+}} + 2\lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-} = y$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}) = \lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-} = z$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives:
$x - y = 2\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - 2\lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-}$
$\Rightarrow \lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-} = \dfrac{x - y}{2}$

The limiting molar conductivity for $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is:
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = \lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-}$

This can be rewritten as:
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = (\lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-}) + (\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-})$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = z + \dfrac{x - y}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{x - y}{2} + z$

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}) = \lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-} = z$

Subtracting the second equation from the first gives:
$x - y = 2\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - 2\lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-}$

$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = (\lambda^0_{\text{NH}_4^+} + \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-}) + (\lambda^0_{\text{OH}^-} - \lambda^0_{\text{Cl}^-})$
$\Lambda_m^0(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}) = z + \dfrac{x - y}{2}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A current of $9.65 \mathrm{~A}$ is passed through dilute sulphuric acid for 10 minutes. The volume of oxygen gas evolved at the anode at STP is:
(Given: $1 \mathrm{~F} = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$, Molar volume of gas at STP $= 22400 \mathrm{~mL} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis, the total charge passed is:
$Q = I \times t$
$Q = 9.65 \mathrm{~A} \times (10 \times 60) \mathrm{~s} = 5790 \mathrm{~C}$

Number of moles of electrons passed $= \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{5790}{96500} = 0.06 \mathrm{~mol}$

The reaction at the anode for the evolution of oxygen is:
$2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}) \rightarrow \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-}$

From the stoichiometry, 4 moles of electrons produce 1 mole of $\mathrm{O}_2$ gas.
Moles of $\mathrm{O}_2$ produced $= \dfrac{0.06}{4} = 0.015 \mathrm{~mol}$

Volume of $\mathrm{O}_2$ at STP $= 0.015 \mathrm{~mol} \times 22400 \mathrm{~mL} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} = 336 \mathrm{~mL}$

Answer: $336 \mathrm{~mL}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For the galvanic cell reaction involving magnesium and silver:
$\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{s})+2 \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+2 \mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})$
The standard Gibbs energy change ($\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ}$) is $-617.6 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. If the standard reduction potential of the $\mathrm{Ag}^{+} / \mathrm{Ag}$ electrode is $0.80 \mathrm{~V}$, what is the standard reduction potential of the $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}$ electrode?
(Given $1 \mathrm{~F}=96500 \mathrm{~C} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The given cell reaction is:
$\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{s})+2 \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})+2 \mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})$

The number of moles of electrons transferred is $n = 2$.

The standard Gibbs energy change is:
$\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -n \mathrm{F} \mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}$
$-617.6 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} = -2 \times 96500 \mathrm{~C} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \times \mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ}$

$\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ} = \dfrac{-617600}{-193000} \mathrm{~V} = 3.20 \mathrm{~V}$

The standard cell potential is also given by the difference in standard reduction potentials of the cathode and anode:
$\mathrm{E}_{\text{cell}}^{\circ} = \mathrm{E}_{\text{cathode}}^{\circ} - \mathrm{E}_{\text{anode}}^{\circ}$

Here, silver is reduced (cathode) and magnesium is oxidized (anode).
$3.20 \mathrm{~V} = \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+} / \mathrm{Ag}}^{\circ} - \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}}^{\circ}$
$3.20 \mathrm{~V} = 0.80 \mathrm{~V} - \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}}^{\circ}$

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}}^{\circ} = 0.80 \mathrm{~V} - 3.20 \mathrm{~V} = -2.40 \mathrm{~V}$

A sign error in the final step leads to $+2.40 \mathrm{~V}$. Assuming $n=1$ gives $-5.60 \mathrm{~V}$, and adding the potentials gives $+4.00 \mathrm{~V}$.

Answer: $-2.40 \mathrm{~V}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
How much time is required to deposit 6.48 g of silver at the cathode when a current of 9.65 A is passed through an aqueous solution of silver nitrate?
(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Ag} = 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}, 1 \mathrm{~F} = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$)
questions.solution:
The reduction reaction at the cathode for silver nitrate is:
$\mathrm{Ag}^{+} + \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})$

Here, the number of moles of electrons required per mole of Ag is $n = 1$.

According to Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis:
$w = \dfrac{M \times I \times t}{n \times F}$

Rearranging for time ($t$):
$t = \dfrac{w \times n \times F}{M \times I}$

Given:
$w = 6.48 \mathrm{~g}$
$M = 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$I = 9.65 \mathrm{~A}$
$F = 96500 \mathrm{~C}$

Substituting the values into the equation:
$t = \dfrac{6.48 \times 1 \times 96500}{108 \times 9.65}$

$t = \dfrac{6.48}{108} \times 10000 = 0.06 \times 10000 = 600 \mathrm{~s}$

Converting the time into minutes:
Time in minutes = $\dfrac{600}{60} = 10 \mathrm{~min}$.

Answer: 10 min

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The standard reduction potentials ($E^{\circ}$) for four metals P, Q, R, and S are given as follows:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{P}^{2+}/\text{P}} = -2.93\text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{Q}^{2+}/\text{Q}} = -0.74\text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{R}^{2+}/\text{R}} = +0.34\text{ V}$
$E^{\circ}_{\text{S}^{2+}/\text{S}} = +0.80\text{ V}$

Which of the following metals can displace exactly two of the other metals from their respective aqueous salt solutions?
questions.solution:
A metal can displace another metal from its aqueous salt solution if it has a lower (more negative) standard reduction potential than the other metal.

Arranging the metals in increasing order of their standard reduction potentials:
P ($-2.93\text{ V}$) < Q ($-0.74\text{ V}$) < R ($+0.34\text{ V}$) < S ($+0.80\text{ V}$)

Evaluating the displacement capacity of each metal:
- Metal P has the lowest $E^{\circ}$ and can displace Q, R, and S (3 metals).
- Metal Q can displace metals with higher $E^{\circ}$ values than itself, which are R and S (exactly 2 metals).
- Metal R can displace only S (1 metal).
- Metal S has the highest $E^{\circ}$ and cannot displace any of the other metals (0 metals).

Therefore, metal Q is the one that can displace exactly two other metals.

Answer: Q

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : The mass of a substance altered at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed.
Statement II : When the same quantity of electricity is passed through solutions of different electrolytes connected in series, the number of moles of the substances deposited is directly proportional to their chemical equivalent weights.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
Statement I is the exact definition of Faraday's first law of electrolysis, hence it is correct.

Statement II is incorrect. According to Faraday's second law of electrolysis, when the same quantity of electricity is passed through solutions of different electrolytes connected in series, the masses of the substances deposited are directly proportional to their chemical equivalent weights. The number of moles deposited is inversely proportional to the valency ($n$-factor) of the respective ions, not directly proportional to their equivalent weights.

Therefore, Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

Answer: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The conductivity and resistance of four different conductivity cells (P, Q, R, and S) filled with the same electrolyte solution are given in the table below. Assuming the area of cross-section of the electrodes is identical for all the cells, which cell has the maximum distance between its electrodes?

CellConductivity ($\kappa$) / $\text{S cm}^{-1}$Resistance ($R$) / $\Omega$
P$0.05$$20$
Q$0.01$$150$
R$0.02$$90$
S$0.04$$10$
questions.solution:
The cell constant ($G^*$) of a conductivity cell is given by the relation:
$G^* = \dfrac{l}{a} = \kappa \times R$

Since the area of cross-section ($a$) is constant for all cells, the distance between the electrodes ($l$) is directly proportional to the product of conductivity ($\kappa$) and resistance ($R$).

Calculating $\kappa \times R$ for each cell:
For Cell P: $G^* = 0.05 \times 20 = 1.0 \text{ cm}^{-1}$
For Cell Q: $G^* = 0.01 \times 150 = 1.5 \text{ cm}^{-1}$
For Cell R: $G^* = 0.02 \times 90 = 1.8 \text{ cm}^{-1}$
For Cell S: $G^* = 0.04 \times 10 = 0.4 \text{ cm}^{-1}$

Cell R has the maximum value of the cell constant, which means it has the maximum distance between its electrodes.

Answer: Cell R

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given the standard electrode potentials for gold at $298$ K:
$E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}) = +1.40$ V
$E^\circ(\text{Au}^+/\text{Au}) = +1.69$ V

What is the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) for the disproportionation reaction of $\text{Au}^+$?
$3\text{Au}^+ \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2\text{Au}$
questions.solution:
The disproportionation reaction is $3\text{Au}^+ \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2\text{Au}$.
This involves two half-reactions:
Oxidation: $\text{Au}^+ \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2e^-$
Reduction: $\text{Au}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$

First, calculate the standard reduction potential for $\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+$:
$\text{Au}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$, $E^\circ_1 = +1.40$ V, $\Delta G^\circ_1 = -3F(1.40) = -4.20F$
$\text{Au}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$, $E^\circ_2 = +1.69$ V, $\Delta G^\circ_2 = -1F(1.69) = -1.69F$

The target half-reaction is $\text{Au}^{3+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}^+$.
This is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2 = -4.20F - (-1.69F) = -2.51F$
$-2FE^\circ_3 = -2.51F \implies E^\circ_3 = +1.255$ V.
So, $E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+) = +1.255$ V.

Now, calculate $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ for the disproportionation:
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}$
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ(\text{Au}^+/\text{Au}) - E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+)$
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.69 \text{ V} - 1.255 \text{ V} = +0.435$ V.

Answer: $+0.435$ V

The disproportionation reaction is $3\text{Au}^+ \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2\text{Au}$.
This involves two half-reactions:
Oxidation: $\text{Au}^+ \rightarrow \text{Au}^{3+} + 2e^-$
Reduction: $\text{Au}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$

First, calculate the standard reduction potential for $\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+$:
$\text{Au}^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$, $E^\circ_1 = +1.40$ V, $\Delta G^\circ_1 = -3F(1.40) = -4.20F$
$\text{Au}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}$, $E^\circ_2 = +1.69$ V, $\Delta G^\circ_2 = -1F(1.69) = -1.69F$

The target half-reaction is $\text{Au}^{3+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Au}^+$.
This is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2 = -4.20F - (-1.69F) = -2.51F$
$-2FE^\circ_3 = -2.51F \implies E^\circ_3 = +1.255$ V.
So, $E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+) = +1.255$ V.

Now, calculate $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ for the disproportionation:
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}$
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ(\text{Au}^+/\text{Au}) - E^\circ(\text{Au}^{3+}/\text{Au}^+)$
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.69 \text{ V} - 1.255 \text{ V} = +0.435$ V.

Answer: $+0.435$ V

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The limiting molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m^\circ$) of a weak electrolyte like acetic acid cannot be determined accurately by extrapolating the plot of $\Lambda_m$ against $\sqrt{c}$ to zero concentration.
Reason (R): The degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte decreases significantly upon dilution.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true. For weak electrolytes, the plot of $\Lambda_m$ against $\sqrt{c}$ shows a steep increase in molar conductivity at low concentrations. Therefore, it does not yield a straight line that can be extrapolated to zero concentration to find $\Lambda_m^\circ$.

Reason (R) is false. According to Ostwald's dilution law, the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte increases significantly upon dilution, which is the actual reason for the steep increase in molar conductivity at lower concentrations.

Therefore, (A) is true but (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.q:
Given the standard electrode potentials at $298$ K:
$E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}) = +0.34$ V
$E^\circ(\text{Cu}^+/\text{Cu}) = +0.52$ V

The standard electrode potential ($E^\circ$) for the half-cell reaction $\text{Cu}^{2+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}^+$ is:
questions.solution:
The given half-cell reactions are:

$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}$, $E^\circ_1 = +0.34$ V
$\Delta G^\circ_1 = -n_1FE^\circ_1 = -2 \times F \times (0.34) = -0.68F$

$\text{Cu}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}$, $E^\circ_2 = +0.52$ V
$\Delta G^\circ_2 = -n_2FE^\circ_2 = -1 \times F \times (0.52) = -0.52F$

The required half-cell reaction is:
$\text{Cu}^{2+} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}^+$

This reaction is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first reaction:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2$

$-1 \times F \times E^\circ_3 = -0.68F - (-0.52F)$

$-FE^\circ_3 = -0.16F$

$E^\circ_3 = +0.16$ V

Answer: $+0.16$ V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Four unknown metals W, X, Y and Z show the following properties:
(i) Metal W displaces X from its aqueous nitrate solution.
(ii) Metal Y displaces W from its aqueous nitrate solution.
(iii) Metal Z does not displace X from its aqueous nitrate solution.

The correct increasing order of standard reduction potentials of these metals is:
questions.solution:
A metal with a lower standard reduction potential (stronger reducing agent) can displace a metal with a higher standard reduction potential from its aqueous salt solution.

From (i), W displaces X, meaning W is a stronger reducing agent than X. Thus, $E^{\circ}_{W} < E^{\circ}_{X}$.

From (ii), Y displaces W, meaning Y is a stronger reducing agent than W. Thus, $E^{\circ}_{Y} < E^{\circ}_{W}$.

From (iii), Z does not displace X, meaning Z is a weaker reducing agent than X. Thus, $E^{\circ}_{Z} > E^{\circ}_{X}$.

Combining these inequalities, the increasing order of standard reduction potentials is $E^{\circ}_{Y} < E^{\circ}_{W} < E^{\circ}_{X} < E^{\circ}_{Z}$.

Therefore, the correct order is Y < W < X < Z.

Answer: Y < W < X < Z

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A $0.020 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$ solution of a weak base $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is $5\%$ dissociated at $298 \text{ K}$. If the limiting ionic conductivities of $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ ions are $73.4 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $198.6 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively, what is the molar conductivity of the solution?
questions.solution:
Limiting molar conductivity of the weak base $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is given by Kohlrausch's law:

$\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ(\text{NH}_4^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{OH}^-)$
$\Lambda_m^\circ = 73.4 + 198.6 = 272.0 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Degree of dissociation, $\alpha = \dfrac{5}{100} = 0.05$

Since $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$, the molar conductivity is:
$\Lambda_m = \alpha \times \Lambda_m^\circ$
$\Lambda_m = 0.05 \times 272.0 = 13.6 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $13.6 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A conductivity cell is filled with a $0.01\text{ M}$ solution of a weak acid. The resistance of the solution is $2500\text{ }\Omega$ and the cell constant is $0.5\text{ cm}^{-1}$. If the limiting molar conductivity of the weak acid is $400\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$, what is its degree of dissociation?
questions.solution:
First, calculate the conductivity ($\kappa$) of the solution using the cell constant ($G^*$) and resistance ($R$):

$\kappa = \dfrac{G^*}{R} = \dfrac{0.5}{2500} = 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ S cm}^{-1}$

Next, calculate the molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) of the solution:

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{c} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{0.01} = \dfrac{0.2}{0.01} = 20\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$

Finally, calculate the degree of dissociation ($\alpha$):

$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{20}{400} = 0.05$

Answer: $0.05$

questions.q:
Calculate the reduction potential of the half-cell represented below at 298 K:
$\text{Pt (s)} | \text{Cl}_2 \text{(g, 0.1 atm)} | \text{Cl}^{-} \text{(aq, 0.01 M)}$
Given: $E^{\circ}_{\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^{-}} = 1.36$ V, $\dfrac{2.303\ RT}{F} = 0.059$ V
questions.solution:
The corresponding reduction half-cell reaction is:
$\text{Cl}_2 \text{(g)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^{-} \text{(aq)}$

Using the Nernst equation for the reduction potential:
$E = E^{\circ}_{\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^{-}} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{Cl}^{-}]^2}{P_{\text{Cl}_2}}$

Given values:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^{-}} = 1.36$ V
$n = 2$
$[\text{Cl}^{-}] = 0.01$ M $= 10^{-2}$ M
$P_{\text{Cl}_2} = 0.1$ atm $= 10^{-1}$ atm

Substituting the values into the Nernst equation:
$E = 1.36 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{(10^{-2})^2}{10^{-1}}$

$E = 1.36 - 0.0295 \log \dfrac{10^{-4}}{10^{-1}}$

$E = 1.36 - 0.0295 \log (10^{-3})$

$E = 1.36 - 0.0295 \times (-3)$

$E = 1.36 + 0.0885$

$E = 1.4485$ V

Answer: $1.4485$ V

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For the concentration cell $Pt | H_2(1 \text{ bar}) | H^+(pH=3) || H^+(pH=2) | H_2(1 \text{ bar}) | Pt$, the cell potential is positive.
Reason (R): In a concentration cell, the cell potential is positive if the concentration of the active ion in the cathodic half-cell is greater than that in the anodic half-cell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
For a hydrogen concentration cell, the net cell reaction is:
$H^+(\text{cathode}) \rightarrow H^+(\text{anode})$

Using the Nernst equation at $298 \text{ K}$:
$E_{cell} = E^\circ_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{1} \log \dfrac{[H^+]_{\text{anode}}}{[H^+]_{\text{cathode}}}$

Since $E^\circ_{cell} = 0$ for a concentration cell, $E_{cell}$ will be positive only if $\log \dfrac{[H^+]_{\text{anode}}}{[H^+]_{\text{cathode}}} < 0$, which means $[H^+]_{\text{cathode}} > [H^+]_{\text{anode}}$. Thus, Reason (R) is correct.

Evaluating Assertion (A):
At the anode, $pH = 3 \implies [H^+]_{\text{anode}} = 10^{-3} \text{ M}$
At the cathode, $pH = 2 \implies [H^+]_{\text{cathode}} = 10^{-2} \text{ M}$

Since $[H^+]_{\text{cathode}} > [H^+]_{\text{anode}}$, the cell potential $E_{cell}$ is positive. Therefore, Assertion (A) is correct.

Reason (R) correctly explains why the cell potential in Assertion (A) is positive.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Dilute sulphuric acid is electrolysed using platinum electrodes by passing a current of $9.65$ A for $10$ minutes. The volume of oxygen gas liberated at the anode at STP is :
(Given : Molar volume of a gas at STP $= 22.4$ L mol$^{-1}$; $1$ F $= 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The quantity of charge $Q$ passed through the solution is:
$Q = I \times t = 9.65 \text{ A} \times (10 \times 60) \text{ s} = 5790 \text{ C}$

The oxidation reaction at the anode is:
$2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{O}_2(g) + 4\text{H}^{+}(aq) + 4\text{e}^{-}$

This indicates that $4$ moles of electrons ($4$ F of charge) are required to produce $1$ mole of $\text{O}_2$ gas. Thus, the n-factor for oxygen gas evolution is $4$.

Number of moles of $\text{O}_2$ produced $= \dfrac{Q}{n \times F} = \dfrac{5790}{4 \times 96500} = \dfrac{5790}{386000} = 0.015 \text{ mol}$

Volume of $\text{O}_2$ gas at STP $= \text{moles} \times \text{Molar volume}$
$V = 0.015 \text{ mol} \times 22.4 \text{ L mol}^{-1} = 0.336 \text{ L}$

Converting to millilitres:
$V = 0.336 \times 1000 = 336 \text{ mL}$

Answer: $336$ mL

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Consider the theoretical plots of molar conductivity ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$) versus $\sqrt{c}$ for aqueous solutions of $\mathrm{NaCl}$, $\mathrm{KCl}$, and $\mathrm{CaCl}_2$ at $298\text{ K}$. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The plots for $\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{CaCl}_2$ are parallel to each other because both contain chloride ions.
The plots for $\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{KCl}$ have the same intercept on the y-axis because they are the same type of electrolyte.
The plots for $\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{KCl}$ are parallel to each other, but they have different intercepts on the y-axis.
The plots for all three electrolytes have the same slope because they are all strong electrolytes.
questions.solution:
According to the Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation, $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - \mathrm{A} \sqrt{c}$.

The slope of the plot is $-\mathrm{A}$. The value of the constant 'A' depends on the type of electrolyte (charges on the cation and anion).

$\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{KCl}$ are both 1-1 electrolytes, so they have the same value of 'A'. Thus, their plots will have the same slope and be parallel to each other.

The intercept on the y-axis is the limiting molar conductivity ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$). According to Kohlrausch's law, $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$ depends on the specific limiting ionic conductivities of the constituent ions. Since $\mathrm{Na}^+$ and $\mathrm{K}^+$ have different limiting ionic conductivities, $\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{KCl}$ will have different intercepts.

$\mathrm{CaCl}_2$ is a 2-1 electrolyte, so it has a different value of 'A' and its plot will not be parallel to that of $\mathrm{NaCl}$ or $\mathrm{KCl}$.

Answer: The plots for $\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{KCl}$ are parallel to each other, but they have different intercepts on the y-axis.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a generic metal $M$, the standard reduction potentials for the $M^{3+}/M$ and $M^{2+}/M$ couples are given as $x$ and $y$ respectively. The standard electrode potential for the $M^{3+}/M^{2+}$ half-cell reaction will be:
questions.solution:
The given half-cell reactions can be written as:

$M^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow M$, $E^\circ_1 = x$
$\Delta G^\circ_1 = -n_1FE^\circ_1 = -3Fx$

$M^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow M$, $E^\circ_2 = y$
$\Delta G^\circ_2 = -n_2FE^\circ_2 = -2Fy$

The required half-cell reaction is:
$M^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow M^{2+}$

This reaction is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first reaction:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2$

$-1 \times F \times E^\circ_3 = -3Fx - (-2Fy)$

$-FE^\circ_3 = -3Fx + 2Fy$

$E^\circ_3 = \dfrac{3Fx - 2Fy}{F} = 3x - 2y$

Answer: $3x - 2y$

$M^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow M$, $E^\circ_2 = y$
$\Delta G^\circ_2 = -n_2FE^\circ_2 = -2Fy$

The required half-cell reaction is:
$M^{3+} + e^- \rightarrow M^{2+}$

This reaction is obtained by subtracting the second reaction from the first reaction:
$\Delta G^\circ_3 = \Delta G^\circ_1 - \Delta G^\circ_2$

$-1 \times F \times E^\circ_3 = -3Fx - (-2Fy)$

$-FE^\circ_3 = -3Fx + 2Fy$

$E^\circ_3 = \dfrac{3Fx - 2Fy}{F} = 3x - 2y$

Answer: $3x - 2y$

The limiting molar conductivities ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$) of some strong electrolytes are given below:

Electrolyte$\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} / \mathrm{S~cm}^2~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$
$\mathrm{CH_3COONa}$$90$
$\mathrm{HCl}$$425$
$\mathrm{NaCl}$$115$


If the molar conductivity of a $0.02~\mathrm{mol~L}^{-1}$ solution of acetic acid ($\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$) is $48~\mathrm{S~cm}^2~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$, its degree of dissociation is:
questions.solution:
According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions, the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid ($\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$) can be calculated from the given strong electrolytes:

$\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}) + \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) - \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl})$
$\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = 90 + 425 - 115 = 400~\mathrm{S~cm}^2~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

The degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) is the ratio of molar conductivity at a given concentration to the limiting molar conductivity:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}$
$\alpha = \dfrac{48}{400} = 0.12$

Adding all three values incorrectly yields $630$, giving $0.076$. Using only the salt's value yields $0.53$.

Answer: $0.12$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The standard cell potential for the following redox reaction is $0.236\text{ V}$ at $298\text{ K}$:

$2\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{I}_{2}(\text{s})$

The equilibrium constant ($K_{c}$) for this reaction is:

$\left[\text{Given: }\dfrac{2.303\text{ }RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V at }298\text{ K}\right]$
questions.solution:
First, determine the number of electrons transferred ($n$) in the balanced redox reaction. The oxidation half-reaction is $2\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow \text{I}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-}$, and the reduction half-reaction is $2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}$. Thus, $n = 2$.

The relationship between the standard cell potential and the equilibrium constant is:

$E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log K_{c}$

Substitute the given values ($E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0.236\text{ V}$ and $n = 2$):

$0.236 = \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log K_{c}$

$0.236 = 0.0295 \log K_{c}$

$\log K_{c} = \dfrac{0.236}{0.0295} = 8$

$K_{c} = 10^{8}$

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{8}$

questions.q:
The standard Gibbs energy change ($\Delta_{\text{r}}G^{\ominus}$) for the following reaction is $-868.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ :
$2\text{M(s)} + 6\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{M}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 3\text{H}_{2}(\text{g})$
Calculate the standard reduction potential of the $\text{M}^{3+}/\text{M}$ half-cell.
(Given : $1 \text{ F} = 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
For the given balanced reaction, the number of moles of electrons transferred is $n = 6$.

Using the relation:
$\Delta_{\text{r}}G^{\ominus} = -nFE_{\text{cell}}^{\ominus}$
$-868500 \text{ J mol}^{-1} = -6 \times 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1} \times E_{\text{cell}}^{\ominus}$
$E_{\text{cell}}^{\ominus} = \dfrac{868500}{579000} \text{ V} = +1.50 \text{ V}$

The cell consists of the $\text{M}$ anode and the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) as the cathode.
$E_{\text{cell}}^{\ominus} = E_{\text{cathode}}^{\ominus} - E_{\text{anode}}^{\ominus}$
$1.50 \text{ V} = E_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_{2}}^{\ominus} - E_{\text{M}^{3+}/\text{M}}^{\ominus}$
$1.50 \text{ V} = 0 \text{ V} - E_{\text{M}^{3+}/\text{M}}^{\ominus}$
$E_{\text{M}^{3+}/\text{M}}^{\ominus} = -1.50 \text{ V}$

Answer: $-1.50 \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Copper dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid to evolve hydrogen gas.
Reason (R): The standard reduction potential of $\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}$ is positive and higher than that of $\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_{2}$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is false because copper does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid to evolve hydrogen gas. Metals placed above hydrogen in the electrochemical series (having negative standard reduction potentials) can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Copper is placed below hydrogen.

Reason (R) is true because the standard reduction potential of the $\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}$ electrode is $+0.34 \text{ V}$, which is positive and higher than the standard reduction potential of the standard hydrogen electrode ($0.00 \text{ V}$).

Therefore, Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The plots of $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ for aqueous solutions of $\mathrm{BaCl}_2$ and $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ have the same slope at $298\mathrm{~K}$.
Reason (R): $\mathrm{BaCl}_2$ is a 2-1 electrolyte while $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ is a 2-2 electrolyte, hence they have different values for the constant '$A$' in the Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
The variation of molar conductivity ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$) with concentration for strong electrolytes is given by $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - A\sqrt{c}$.

The slope of the $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ plot is $-A$. The value of the constant '$A$' depends on the type of electrolyte, which is determined by the valency of the cation and anion produced on dissociation.

$\mathrm{BaCl}_2$ dissociates into $\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}$ and $2\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, making it a 2-1 electrolyte.
$\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ dissociates into $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}$, making it a 2-2 electrolyte.

Since they are different types of electrolytes, they have different values for the constant '$A$'. Therefore, their plots will have different slopes.

Thus, Assertion (A) is not correct, but Reason (R) is correct.

Answer: (A) is not correct but (R) is correct

$\text{KNO}_3$$145$
$\text{KA}$$104$


The molar conductivity of a $0.02\text{ M}$ solution of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ is $19\text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$. What is the dissociation constant ($K_a$) of the weak acid $\text{HA}$? (Assume $1 - \alpha \approx 1$)
questions.solution:
According to Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions:

$\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HA}) = \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HNO}_3) + \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{KA}) - \Lambda_m^\circ(\text{KNO}_3)$

$\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HA}) = 421 + 104 - 145 = 380\text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

The degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) is given by:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} = \dfrac{19}{380} = 0.05$

The dissociation constant ($K_a$) is calculated as:

$K_a = c\alpha^2$

$K_a = 0.02 \times (0.05)^2$

$K_a = 0.02 \times 0.0025 = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}$

Answer: $5.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A conductivity cell with a cell constant of $0.4 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is filled with a $0.02 \text{ M}$ solution of an electrolyte. If the measured resistance of the cell is $100 \text{ }\Omega$, the molar conductivity of the solution is:
questions.solution:
First, calculate the conductivity ($\kappa$) of the solution using the cell constant ($G^*$) and resistance ($R$):

$\kappa = \dfrac{G^*}{R} = \dfrac{0.4 \text{ cm}^{-1}}{100 \text{ }\Omega} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ S cm}^{-1}$

Next, calculate the molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) using the formula:

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}$

Substituting the values:

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-3} \times 1000}{0.02} = \dfrac{4}{0.02} = 200 \text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $200 \text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For strong electrolytes, the molar conductivity ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$) varies with concentration according to the linear equation $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - A\sqrt{c}$. Which of the following statements correctly describes the behaviour of a weak electrolyte, such as acetic acid, under similar dilution conditions?
options: Its molar conductivity increases steeply at lower concentrations, and its $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$ cannot be obtained by extrapolating the plot to zero concentration.
It follows the same linear equation as strong electrolytes, but with a significantly larger value of the constant '$A$'.
Its molar conductivity decreases upon dilution because the degree of dissociation is suppressed at lower concentrations.
Its $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ plot is a straight line that passes through the origin.
questions.solution:
For weak electrolytes like acetic acid, the degree of dissociation increases significantly upon dilution.

As a result, the number of ions in the solution increases, leading to a steep increase in molar conductivity ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$) at lower concentrations. Because of this steep curve, the plot of $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ versus $\sqrt{c}$ is not linear.

Consequently, the limiting molar conductivity ($\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$) for weak electrolytes cannot be obtained by simply extrapolating the curve to zero concentration (as is done for strong electrolytes). Instead, Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions is used.

Therefore, the correct description is that its molar conductivity increases steeply at lower concentrations and its $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$ cannot be obtained by extrapolation.

Answer: Its molar conductivity increases steeply at lower concentrations, and its $\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}$ cannot be obtained by extrapolating the plot to zero concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two electrolytic cells containing aqueous solutions of $\mathrm{CuSO}_4$ and $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ respectively are connected in series. If $1.27 \mathrm{~g}$ of copper is deposited at the cathode of the first cell, what will be the mass of silver deposited at the cathode of the second cell?
(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{Cu} = 63.5 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$, $\mathrm{Ag} = 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
According to Faraday's Second Law of Electrolysis, when the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes connected in series, the masses of the substances deposited are proportional to their respective equivalent weights.

$\dfrac{w_{\mathrm{Ag}}}{w_{\mathrm{Cu}}} = \dfrac{E_{\mathrm{Ag}}}{E_{\mathrm{Cu}}}$

The equivalent weight of a metal is its molar mass divided by its valency (n-factor).
For $\mathrm{Ag}$ in $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$, valency $= 1$
$E_{\mathrm{Ag}} = \dfrac{108}{1} = 108$

For $\mathrm{Cu}$ in $\mathrm{CuSO}_4$, valency $= 2$
$E_{\mathrm{Cu}} = \dfrac{63.5}{2} = 31.75$

Substituting the values into the ratio:
$\dfrac{w_{\mathrm{Ag}}}{1.27} = \dfrac{108}{31.75}$

$w_{\mathrm{Ag}} = 1.27 \times \dfrac{108}{31.75} = 1.27 \times 3.4015...$

Alternatively, calculate the number of equivalents of Cu deposited:
Equivalents of $\mathrm{Cu} = \dfrac{1.27}{31.75} = 0.04$

Equivalents of $\mathrm{Ag}$ deposited $= 0.04$
Mass of $\mathrm{Ag} = 0.04 \times 108 = 4.32 \mathrm{~g}$

Answer: $4.32 \mathrm{~g}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a weak monobasic acid at concentration $C$, the acid dissociation constant $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is given by the expression $K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C (\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ})^2}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}} (\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}})}$.

Reason (R): The degree of dissociation $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}$ and according to Ostwald's dilution law, $K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
The Reason statement correctly provides the standard formulas for the degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) in terms of molar conductivities and the acid dissociation constant ($K_{\mathrm{a}}$) from Ostwald's dilution law. Therefore, Reason (R) is true.

To evaluate the Assertion, substitute $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}$ into the expression for $K_{\mathrm{a}}$:

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \left(\dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}\right)^2}{1 - \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}}$

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^2}{(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ})^2}}{\dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}}$

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^2}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} (\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}})}$

The expression given in the Assertion has the numerator and denominator terms incorrectly swapped, making Assertion (A) false.

Answer: Assertion is false but Reason is true.

Assertion (A): For a weak monobasic acid at concentration $C$, the acid dissociation constant $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is given by the expression $K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C (\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ})^2}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}} (\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}})}$.

Reason (R): The degree of dissociation $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}$ and according to Ostwald's dilution law, $K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The Reason statement correctly provides the standard formulas for the degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) in terms of molar conductivities and the acid dissociation constant ($K_{\mathrm{a}}$) from Ostwald's dilution law. Therefore, Reason (R) is true.

To evaluate the Assertion, substitute $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}$ into the expression for $K_{\mathrm{a}}$:

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \left(\dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}\right)^2}{1 - \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}}$

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^2}{(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ})^2}}{\dfrac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ}}}$

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{C \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^2}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} (\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}^{\circ} - \Lambda_{\mathrm{m}})}$

The expression given in the Assertion has the numerator and denominator terms incorrectly swapped, making Assertion (A) false.

Answer: Assertion is false but Reason is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A $0.1\text{ M}$ solution of a hypothetical weak acid $\text{HA}$ has a dissociation constant of $1.0 \times 10^{-5}$. The limiting ionic conductivities of $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{A}^-$ are $350\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$ and $50\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. What is the molar conductivity of the solution?
questions.solution:
The limiting molar conductivity of the weak acid $\text{HA}$ is given by Kohlrausch's law:

$\Lambda_m^\circ = \lambda^\circ_{\text{H}^+} + \lambda^\circ_{\text{A}^-} = 350 + 50 = 400\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$

For a weak acid, the degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) is related to the dissociation constant ($K_a$) and concentration ($c$) by $K_a \approx c\alpha^2$ (since $\alpha$ is very small).

$\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_a}{c}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-5}}{0.1}} = \sqrt{10^{-4}} = 0.01$

The molar conductivity ($\Lambda_m$) is related to $\alpha$ by:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}$

$\Lambda_m = \alpha \times \Lambda_m^\circ = 0.01 \times 400 = 4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$

Answer: $4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a balanced equation for a galvanic cell reaction is multiplied by 2, the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) is also doubled.

Reason (R): Standard cell potential is an intensive property, whereas standard Gibbs energy change ($\Delta_r G^\circ$) is an extensive property.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is false. When a balanced cell reaction is multiplied by an integer, the standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) remains the same. It does not get multiplied because it is an intensive property (representing energy per unit charge).

Reason (R) is true. Standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) is an intensive thermodynamic property, meaning it is independent of the amount of substance reacting. In contrast, standard Gibbs energy change ($\Delta_r G^\circ$) is an extensive property, which means its value depends on the amount of substance and will be multiplied if the stoichiometric coefficients are multiplied.

Therefore, (A) is false but (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Find the oxidation potential of a hydrogen electrode placed in a $0.1$ M solution of a weak monoprotic acid (HA) with $K_a = 10^{-5}$ at 298 K. The pressure of $\text{H}_2$ gas is maintained at $1$ atm.
$\left(\text{Given}: \dfrac{2.303\ RT}{F} = 0.059\right)$
questions.solution:
First, calculate the hydrogen ion concentration $[\text{H}^{+}]$ for the weak monoprotic acid using Ostwald's dilution law:
$[\text{H}^{+}] = \sqrt{K_a \times C}$
$[\text{H}^{+}] = \sqrt{10^{-5} \times 0.1} = \sqrt{10^{-6}} = 10^{-3}$ M

The oxidation half-cell reaction for the hydrogen electrode is:
$\text{H}_2 \text{(g)} \rightarrow 2\text{H}^{+} \text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-}$

Using the Nernst equation for the oxidation potential:
$E = E^{\circ}_{\text{H}_2/\text{H}^{+}} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log \dfrac{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}{P_{\text{H}_2}}$

Given values:
$E^{\circ}_{\text{H}_2/\text{H}^{+}} = 0$ V
$n = 2$
$[\text{H}^{+}] = 10^{-3}$ M
$P_{\text{H}_2} = 1$ atm

Substituting the values into the Nernst equation:
$E = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{1}$

$E = -0.0295 \log (10^{-6})$

$E = -0.0295 \times (-6)$

$E = +0.177$ V

Answer: $+0.177$ V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-IList-II
(A) $F_2$(I) Strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution
(B) $Li$(II) Standard reference electrode with $0.00\text{ V}$
(C) $H^+$(III) Strongest oxidizing agent
(D) $Zn$(IV) Can reduce $Cu^{2+}$ but not $Mg^{2+}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
According to the electrochemical series:

Fluorine ($F_2$) has the highest standard reduction potential ($+2.87\text{ V}$), making it the strongest oxidizing agent.

Lithium ($Li$) has the lowest standard reduction potential ($-3.05\text{ V}$), making it the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solutions.

The Standard Hydrogen Electrode ($H^+$) is assigned a standard reduction potential of exactly $0.00\text{ V}$.

Zinc ($Zn$) has a standard reduction potential of $-0.76\text{ V}$, which is lower than that of Copper ($+0.34\text{ V}$) but higher than that of Magnesium ($-2.36\text{ V}$). Therefore, $Zn$ can reduce $Cu^{2+}$ but cannot reduce $Mg^{2+}$.

Thus, the correct match is (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider a hydrogen reduction electrode represented as $\text{H}^{+} \text{(aq)} | \text{H}_2 \text{(g)} | \text{Pt}$. Read the following four statements regarding its reduction potential at $298$ K:
I. The reduction potential increases (becomes less negative) as the pH of the solution decreases at constant pressure.
II. The reduction potential becomes more negative if the pressure of $\text{H}_2$ gas is increased at constant pH.
III. At $\text{pH} = 10$ and $P_{\text{H}_2} = 1$ atm, the reduction potential is $-0.59$ V.
IV. If the solution is diluted $10$ times, the oxidation potential of the electrode decreases by $59$ mV.

How many of the given statements are correct?
$\left(\text{Given}: \dfrac{2.303\ RT}{F} = 0.059\right)$
questions.solution:
The reduction half-reaction is: $2\text{H}^{+} \text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2 \text{(g)}$

Using the Nernst equation for reduction potential:
$E_{\text{red}} = E^{\circ} - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log \dfrac{P_{\text{H}_2}}{[\text{H}^{+}]^2}$
$E_{\text{red}} = -0.059 \text{ pH} - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log P_{\text{H}_2}$

Statement I: As pH decreases, the term $-0.059 \text{ pH}$ becomes less negative, so the reduction potential increases. (Correct)

Statement II: As $P_{\text{H}_2}$ increases, the term $-\dfrac{0.059}{2} \log P_{\text{H}_2}$ becomes more negative, decreasing the reduction potential. (Correct)

Statement III: At $\text{pH} = 10$ and $P_{\text{H}_2} = 1$ atm:
$E_{\text{red}} = -0.059 \times 10 - 0 = -0.59$ V. (Correct)

Statement IV: The oxidation potential is the negative of the reduction potential:
$E_{\text{ox}} = 0.059 \text{ pH} + \dfrac{0.059}{2} \log P_{\text{H}_2}$
Diluting the solution $10$ times decreases $[\text{H}^{+}]$ by a factor of $10$, which increases the pH by $1$.
New $E_{\text{ox}} = 0.059 (\text{pH} + 1) + \dots = E_{\text{ox}} + 0.059$ V.
The oxidation potential increases by $59$ mV, not decreases. (Incorrect)

Therefore, statements I, II, and III are correct. A total of 3 statements are correct.

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The limiting molar conductivities of $\text{HCOONa}$, $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{NaCl}$ are $100$, $425$ and $125 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$ respectively. If the molar conductivity of a $0.01 \text{ M}$ solution of $\text{HCOOH}$ is $40 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$, what is its degree of dissociation?
questions.solution:
According to Kohlrausch's law, the limiting molar conductivity of $\text{HCOOH}$ is calculated from the strong electrolytes as follows:
$\Lambda^\circ_m(\text{HCOOH}) = \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{HCOONa}) + \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{HCl}) - \Lambda^\circ_m(\text{NaCl})$
$\Lambda^\circ_m(\text{HCOOH}) = 100 + 425 - 125 = 400 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$

The degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) is given by the ratio of molar conductivity at a given concentration to the limiting molar conductivity:
$\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^\circ_m}$
$\alpha = \dfrac{40}{400} = 0.1$

Answer: $0.1$
